title: The Great Reading Recession
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick examines the grim reading results in PISA 2025 and rejects the two most common explanations, screens and the pandemic, arguing the decline in sustained-text reading began around 2012, well before either factor could account for it, and that heavy smartphone use in Singapore coexists with the world's highest reading scores. His central diagnostic tool is PISA's 'hasty reader' metric, students who make errors on the opening fluency task yet finish faster than 99% of accurate readers, which he reads as evidence of a specific learned strategy, scanning for a plausible answer and moving on, rather than declining cognitive capacity. He traces this strategy directly to decades of skills-based reading instruction that taught students the question stem and generic comparison-and-inference moves mattered more than the specific text in front of them, making Frankenstein and a four-paragraph pop-culture article functionally interchangeable under that model. Citing Maryanne Wolf's argument that deep reading is a culturally sustained disposition rather than a biological given, and college professors' reports that some students now arrive having never finished a whole book, Hendrick argues declining textual difficulty and skills-first pedagogy, not screens or diminished brains, explain why sustained reading has become a devalued commodity for a generation of students. He closes by rejecting both the 'kids are getting dimmer' framing and reflexive screen-blaming as equally lazy alternatives to confronting what schools actually chose to value.
points: Uses the specific PISA counter-example of Singapore, high smartphone saturation combined with the world's highest reading scores, to directly undercut the screens-caused-the-decline explanation before it can be assumed.

Deploys PISA's 'hasty reader' metric precisely: students who both err on the opening fluency task and finish faster than 99% of accurate peers, arguing this behavioral signature reveals a learned test-taking strategy (scan, guess, move on) rather than a cognitive deficit.

Traces the hasty-reading pattern to a specific pedagogical cause: decades of instruction treating comprehension as generic, transferable skills (find the main idea, infer, compare and contrast) applied to any text, making the specific text itself a secondary consideration.

Cites Nicholas Dames's report of a first-year college student who had never been required to read an entire book in public high school, only excerpts and articles, as direct evidence that declining textual demand, not screens, is degrading sustained-reading capacity.

Rejects both 'kids are getting dimmer' alarmism and reflexive screen-blaming as equally reductive, arguing the actual explanatory variable is that schools implicitly taught students what they read matters less than how they read it.
quotes: If it were all down to the screens then you have to account for the fact that Singapore has among the highest smart-phone saturation in the world but also the highest reading scores.

We are seeing a generation of kids who are not less cognitively capable but rather one raised in a culture of skills-based reading which implicitly told them that what you read is less important than how you read it.

Hasty reading doesn't mean kids who read quicker or students who get wrong answers but rather a kind of deadly combination of the two. It means students who are giving answers to questions that they haven't really spent enough time on to answer them correctly or accurately.
Under this model, Frankenstein and a four paragraph article about KPop Demon Hunters become interchangeable.
In Reader, Come Home, Maryanne Wolf made the claim that the human disposition of deep-reading is something established and sustained by a culture, not determined by our biology

Nicholas Dames reports that a first-year student in Fall 2022 told him her public high school had never required them to read an entire book from beginning to end. Just excerpts, poetry, and articles.

reading comprehension is not predominantly a skill, it is the visible layer of a much deeper set of competencies based on domain knowledge, reading fluency and a set of cultural and environmental norms which value sustained attention to particular texts
